text:
A Next.js MVP for evidence intake,
integrity checks, and custody review.

Local prototype today.
Blockchain anchoring is a future step.

Introduce the project as it exists today: a Next.js evidence-management MVP. It creates browser-local SHA-256 fingerprints and a hash-linked custody sequence. It does not write to a blockchain network.
A file is useful only when its identity and handling context stay with it.
Names can be changed. A cryptographic fingerprint gives the file contents a repeatable identifier.
Without a trusted reference, a later copy is difficult to compare with the one first collected.
The case needs a time-ordered account of intake and later evidence actions.
The vault connects the file, its fingerprint, its case, and its custody record.

Frame the problem around three questions that investigators need to answer: which exact file was collected, whether its contents still match, and what handling actions were recorded. The MVP addresses these questions at a prototype level.

title: The MVP connects a file to its history

text: The MVP connects a file to its history
An evidence record brings together the item, its fingerprint, and its custody events.
Today, the browser stores both the uploaded file and its record. No blockchain transaction is made.

Walk through the product model from left to right. A file upload is associated with case details; the file is fingerprinted; a record stores its metadata; custody events form the history. The storage and hash sequence are local to the browser in this MVP.
Adding an item starts a record that can be searched and reviewed.
Choose a file from the device. The MVP saves its contents in browser storage.
Enter a case ID and choose a category such as document, image, video, or log file.
The browser reads the file bytes and calculates a SHA-256 digest.
The app records intake, hash verification, and sealing events for the item.

Describe the upload interaction shown in the MVP. New evidence is saved locally, and a SHA-256 digest is generated in the browser. The custody entries are created by the application; the current prototype does not capture a cryptographic identity for the actor.
The file hash identifies bytes; the event hash links one custody entry to the next.
A digest to compare the file against later
Changing an earlier link breaks the sequence
A matching hash compares bytes. It does not prove who collected them or whether the process was lawful.

Clarify the distinction. The evidence fingerprint is calculated from file bytes. A custody-event hash includes the prior event hash and evidence digest. Together they allow a later comparison against the stored reference data, but a hash alone cannot establish provenance or collection conditions.

title: Custody events form a linked sequence

text: Custody events form a linked sequence
Each new event points back to the previous event hash.
An event records an action, actor label, timestamp, description, evidence hash, previous hash, and current hash.

In this MVP, the sequence is stored in browser data. A person who can edit that data can also replace the hashes, so the record is tamper-evident only when compared with a separately protected reference.

The three boxes show the local event sequence used for new uploads. Explain that the second event uses the first event hash as its previous value, and the third uses the second. The browser stores the events, so the local copy is not an independently protected blockchain ledger.
The record keeps case context beside the file fingerprint and custody trail.

id: evidence identifier
name: original filename
kind: file extension
category: evidence type
size: file size in bytes
hash: SHA-256 fingerprint
added: intake date and time
owner: uploader label
status: Verified or Pending
caseId: investigation identifier
custody: ordered event list
Name, case, category, size, uploader, date, and verification status make items easier to find and review.
Actions, actor labels, timestamps, and linked hashes show how the item was handled in the local record.

The fields correspond to the evidence record shape used in the MVP. The object has metadata and an ordered custody array. The schema view is explanatory; the slide does not show an actual user's case data.

title: The current architecture stays in the browser

text: The current architecture stays in the browser
The MVP has no application server, shared database, or blockchain connection.
Dashboard, upload form, evidence detail, search and filters
Identity, shared cases, secure storage, durable audit
No transaction or on-chain evidence hash is created today.

Describe the actual MVP architecture: a Next.js and React interface, browser Web Crypto for hashes, IndexedDB for file blobs, and LocalStorage for records. The two right-side components are not implemented; they identify what would need to be added for a production system.

title: A local hash chain is not a blockchain

text: A local hash chain is not a blockchain
The prototype demonstrates verification logic, not a production trust model.

SHA-256 fingerprints for uploaded files

A visible sequence of custody events

Checks against data stored in this browser

A clear message when a sample file is unavailable

Authenticated users and case permissions

Encrypted, durable evidence storage

Independently protected audit records

Optional blockchain anchoring of selected hashes
A hash match checks file bytes against a reference. It does not prove collection, identity, or lawful handling.

Be precise about the trust boundary. The local hash chain is useful to demonstrate the mechanics but it can be edited along with browser data. A production blockchain anchor could help protect a published commitment, but it would not independently prove how the evidence was collected or handled before submission.

title: A practical path to a production vault

text: A practical path to a production vault
Build the evidence controls first. Anchor only protected records.
Add authentication and case roles. Move evidence and metadata into encrypted, durable storage.
Add an append-only audit service, backups, retention rules, and exportable verification reports.
Choose a network and publish evidence commitments with transaction receipts and independent checks.
The current deliverable is the first workflow prototype, not the completed production system.

Close with a staged development path. First establish identity and secure storage. Then protect and export the audit history. Only after those controls exist should the project decide whether blockchain anchoring is useful, and which hashes are appropriate to publish.
